pr.title: Fix generator and analyzer crash on closed generic struct from a referenced assembly (REQ-2283)
pr.body:
Requirement: REQ-2283

Agent-written implementation of requirement REQ-2283 (upstream MessagePack-CSharp issue 2283), from the Junction 2026 challenge branch `ju26-issue-2283`.

Author: coding agent. Accountable owner: to be assigned by Countersign.
pr.author: ToukoUrsin

requirement.title: Generator and analyzer crash with IndexOutOfRangeException on a closed generic struct from a referenced assembly
requirement.body:
#### Bug description

Both `MessagePackGenerator` (CS8785) and `MsgPack00xMessagePackAnalyzer` (AD0001) throw `IndexOutOfRangeException` when a `[MessagePackObject]` type has a member whose type is a **closed generic value type defined in a referenced assembly**.

Because the generator then "will not contribute to the output", the compiling assembly silently ends up with **no generated resolver at all**. It is only a warning, so a normal build looks fine, but trimmed and NativeAOT apps fail at runtime. In our case three assemblies of a large app had been shipping without a resolver across two releases before we noticed.

#### Repro steps

Two projects. `lib`:

```csharp
using MessagePack;
namespace Lib;

[MessagePackObject]
public partial record struct Item<T>([property: Key(0)] string Key);
```

`app`, with a `ProjectReference` to `lib`:

```csharp
using MessagePack; using Lib;
namespace App;

[MessagePackObject]
public sealed partial record Cmd([property: Key(0)] string Scope)
{
    [Key(1)] public Item<int> Member { get; init; }
}
```

Then `dotnet build` on `app`. Both projects are in the attached `mp-repro.zip`.

#### Expected behavior

A clean build, with a generated resolver in `app`.
#### Actual behavior

```
CSC : warning CS8785: Generator 'MessagePackGenerator' failed to generate source. It will not
contribute to the output and compilation errors may occur as a result. Exception was of type
'IndexOutOfRangeException' with message 'Index was outside the bounds of the array.'.
CSC : warning AD0001: Analyzer 'MessagePack.SourceGenerator.Analyzers.MsgPack00xMessagePackAnalyzer'
threw an exception of type 'System.IndexOutOfRangeException' with message 'Index was outside the
bounds of the array.'.
```

`app.dll` contains no `GeneratedMessagePackResolver`.

- Version used: MessagePack 3.1.8
- Runtime: .NET 10 (SDK 10.0.204), Windows 11

#### Additional context

**What triggers it.** `Item` is declared in `lib`, `Cmd` in `app`:

| `Item` declared as | result |
|---|---|
| `record struct Item<T>` | **crash** |
| `struct Item<T>` | **crash** |
| `struct Item` | ok |
| `record struct Item` | ok |
| `class Item<T>` | ok |
| `record class Item<T>` | ok |

So it needs all three of: **generic**, **value type**, **from a referenced assembly**. Moving the identical `Item<T>` declaration into `app` itself makes the crash disappear, which is what makes this specific to metadata symbols.
**Stack trace.**

```
System.IndexOutOfRangeException: Index was outside the bounds of the array.
   at TypeCollector.GetObjectInfo(INamedTypeSymbol formattedType, ISymbol callerSymbol)
   at TypeCollector.CollectGeneric(INamedTypeSymbol type, ISymbol callerSymbol) in TypeCollector.cs:line 661
   at TypeCollector.CollectCore(ITypeSymbol typeSymbol, ISymbol callerSymbol) in TypeCollector.cs:line 371
   at TypeCollector.GetObjectInfo(INamedTypeSymbol formattedType, ISymbol callerSymbol) in TypeCollector.cs:line 1062
   at TypeCollector.CollectCore(ITypeSymbol typeSymbol, ISymbol callerSymbol) in TypeCollector.cs:line 386
   at TypeCollector.Collect() in TypeCollector.cs:line 300
   at MsgPack00xMessagePackAnalyzer.AnalyzeSymbol(SymbolAnalysisContext, ReferenceSymbols, AnalyzerOptions) in MsgPack00xMessagePackAnalyzer.cs:line 431
```

`CollectGeneric` line 661 is the closed-generic branch that calls `GetObjectInfo` directly:

```csharp
else
{
    // NOTE: ... closed generic types such as `Foo<string>` are not registered as a formatter.
    this.GetObjectInfo(type, callerSymbol);
```

so `GetObjectInfo` runs against a type that has no syntax. Several diagnostic paths inside it index `DeclaringSyntaxReferences[0]` directly (lines 735, 1009, 1101) instead of using `FirstOrDefault()` the way the neighbouring `GetIdentifierLocation` / `GetLocation` / `GetParameterListLocation` helpers already do, and that collection is empty for a metadata symbol. I did not narrow down which of the three fires.

**Getting the stack trace.** Console output truncates the exception to its message; `-p:ErrorLog=out.sarif` preserves the full description, including the stack trace and an `ISymbol:` context line naming the offending type:

```
dotnet build -p:ErrorLog=out.sarif
```

**Workaround.** Putting `[MessagePackFormatter(typeof(ItemFormatter<>))]` on the generic value type short-circuits `CollectCore` (line 356) before `GetObjectInfo` is reached, at the cost of hand-writing the formatter.

**Possibly related:** #2092 reports CS8785 from the v3 generator, but with a different inner exception and no repro.

[mp-repro.zip](https://github.com/user-attachments/files/30408133/mp-repro.zip)

story.headline: The MessagePack generator and analyzer no longer crash when a [MessagePackObject] type has a member whose type is a closed generic struct from a referenced assembly, so the app assembly again gets its generated resolver.
story.before: When a member's type was a closed generic value type such as Item<int> from another assembly, TypeCollector.GetObjectInfo read DeclaringSyntaxReferences[0] on a symbol that has no source. That threw IndexOutOfRangeException. The generator reported CS8785 and produced no resolver, and the analyzer reported AD0001.
story.after: The places that indexed [0] now use FirstOrDefault or a null-returning helper, so the generator completes and emits the resolver. Analyzer diagnostics pass through a filter that only reports those located in a source tree of the current compilation. Diagnostics about members of referenced-assembly types are therefore not reported in the consuming project.

steps.text: In TypeCollector.GetObjectInfo, two diagnostic sites that read DeclaringSyntaxReferences[0] now use FirstOrDefault or the new GetPropertyIdentifierLocation helper. For metadata members these return a null location instead of throwing. This is the fix for the generator crash, because the generator builds Diagnostic objects even when it does not report them.

The TypeCollector constructor wraps the analyzer's report callback in ReportIfLocatedInCompilation. The wrapper forwards a diagnostic only if its location is in source and in a syntax tree of the compilation. All other diagnostics are dropped, including those with no location. The same hunk defines GetPropertyIdentifierLocation.

Three new tests build a defining assembly into an image and reference it as metadata only. The cases are a generic struct, a generic record struct, and a struct with an unkeyed member. Each test expects no diagnostics from the analyzer and the generator, and checks that the resolver source file is generated.

The README says closed generic types from referenced assemblies are supported. The README and the MsgPack004 docs say that diagnostics about members of those types are reported only by the assembly that defines them.

alsoTouches: The location filter applies to every analyzer diagnostic raised through TypeCollector, not only those for referenced-assembly types, so any diagnostic with a null or out-of-compilation location is now dropped.
Error-level diagnostics such as a missing key on a member of a referenced generic struct are no longer shown in the consuming project.

GetPropertyIdentifierLocation returns null for positional record properties, because their syntax is a parameter rather than a PropertyDeclarationSyntax, so MsgPack005 raised on such a property in source is now dropped by the filter.
The generator path (reportAnalyzerDiagnostic null) is unchanged apart from the null-safe location lookups.

diagrams.title: Null-safe member locations and an in-compilation diagnostic filter in TypeCollector
diagrams.caption: Both the generator and the analyzer reach GetObjectInfo through TypeCollector. U1 stops the crash for both, and U2 adds a filter that applies only to the analyzer's diagnostics.

diagrams.title: Building app with a Cmd.Member of type Item<int> from lib
diagrams.caption: Before, GetObjectInfo threw while building a diagnostic location. Now the location is null, the generator emits the resolver, and the analyzer's filter drops the diagnostic.

units.title: Look up member diagnostic locations without indexing syntax refs
units.summary: Two places in TypeCollector used to index `DeclaringSyntaxReferences[0]`, which throws for members that come from a referenced assembly because they have no source syntax. They now use FirstOrDefault or the new GetPropertyIdentifierLocation helper (defined in hunk F3.H4), which returns null when there is no source. The generator calls TypeCollector with reportAnalyzerDiagnostic set to null, but it still builds these Diagnostic objects, so this change is what stops the generator's IndexOutOfRangeException (CS8785).

lines.s: Learn more about using a mix of your own custom formatters and automatically generated ones in [the Analyzer section](#analyzer).

Closed generic types defined in a referenced assembly (for example, `Item<int>` where `Item<T>` is defined in another project or NuGet package) can be used as members of your `[MessagePackObject]` types, including generic value types and record structs.
Diagnostics about the members of such a type are reported by the assembly that defines it rather than by the consuming project, so any problem must be fixed there.

[MagicOnion](https://github.com/Cysharp/MagicOnion) is a code-first gRPC framework based on grpc-dotnet and MessagePack. gRPC usually communicates with Protocol Buffers using IDL. But MagicOnion uses MessagePack for C# and does not need IDL. When communicating C# to C#, schemaless (or rather C# classes as schema) is better than using IDL.
This analyzer only reports on members declared in the project being compiled.
Members of a type defined in a referenced assembly are reported by the project that defines that type, so an unattributed public member of such a type must be fixed in its defining project.

findings.title: New filter silently drops Error-level diagnostics for referenced-assembly generic types
findings.body: Every diagnostic TypeCollector reports to the analyzer now passes through ReportIfLocatedInCompilation, which discards anything without a source location in the current compilation, including Location.None. The crash only needed the `[0]` index at the field MemberNeedsKey site fixed (F3.H3); the filter is a separate, wider behaviour change. Sites that already used FirstOrDefault (for example the property MemberNeedsKey at line 930) previously surfaced an Error-severity MsgPack004 without a location; those are now silent. The consuming project still generates its own formatter for the referenced generic definition (line 654), so the unkeyed member is left out of serialization with no build signal.
findings.scenario: lib defines `[MessagePackObject] public struct MyGenericStruct<T> { [Key(0)] public string Key {get;set;} public int Unkeyed {get;set;} }` and is built without the MessagePack analyzer (as the PR's own test does). app has a `[Key(0)] MyGenericStruct<int>` member. Result: app builds with zero diagnostics and `Unkeyed` is not serialized. A generic class from a referenced assembly with the same shape did not hit the crash path per the requirement's table, so by reading the code it would have produced MsgPack004 before this change and no longer does (not run).

refs.quote: this.reportDiagnostic = reportAnalyzerDiagnostic is null ? null : diagnostic => ReportIfLocatedInCompilation(reportAnalyzerDiagnostic, diagnostic);

findings.suggestion: Have a human decide the policy first (see refusals). If diagnostics on foreign types should survive, re-anchor them to the consuming member (callerSymbol) or keep Location.None instead of dropping. If dropping is intended, narrow it to the known-noisy case (compiler-generated backing fields from metadata) rather than all diagnostic IDs.

findings.title: MsgPack005 on a positional record property is now silently dropped
findings.body: The new GetPropertyIdentifierLocation only recognises PropertyDeclarationSyntax and returns null for anything else. A source-declared positional record property is declared by a ParameterSyntax, which the neighbouring MemberNeedsKey code at line 926 handles explicitly. A null location becomes Location.None, and the new ReportIfLocatedInCompilation filter discards any diagnostic that is not in source. The old hard cast would have thrown here, so this trades a loud failure for a silent one. I did not run this; it is inferred from reading the code.
findings.scenario: In the compiled project: `[MessagePackObject] public partial record R([property: Key(null)] string X);`. intKey and stringKey are both null, so BothStringAndIntKeyAreNull is created with a null location and filtered out. No MsgPack005 appears, and X is added to neither intMembers nor stringMembers, so it is silently left out of the formatter.

refs.quote: var identifier = (syntax as PropertyDeclarationSyntax)?.Identifier ?? (syntax as ParameterSyntax)?.Identifier;

findings.suggestion: Make GetPropertyIdentifierLocation fall back to the ParameterSyntax identifier (as line 926 does) and then to the syntax node's own location. Add an analyzer test for `[property: Key(null)]` on a positional record.

findings.title: Location filter also drops location-less diagnostics for cases that never crashed
findings.body: ReportIfLocatedInCompilation wraps every diagnostic the collector reports and discards any whose location is not a source tree of this compilation. That covers far more than the three crash sites. Diagnostics about metadata types that were previously reported in the consuming build, at Location.None or a metadata location, are now silent. Generic classes from referenced assemblies never crashed according to the requirement's table, so their diagnostics change too. Meanwhile line 654 still collects the referenced generic definition so a formatter is still generated for it.
findings.scenario: lib: `[MessagePackObject] public class Box<T> { [Key(0)] public T Value { get; set; } public Box(string other) { } }`. app has a `[Key(0)] Box<int>` member. NoDeserializingConstructor is created with GetIdentifierLocation(formattedType), which is null for a metadata type. Before this change the app build showed MsgPack007 without a location; now it shows nothing, and the generator still emits a Box<T> formatter with no usable constructor.
findings.suggestion: Narrow the filter to what is needed: drop only diagnostics whose source tree belongs to another compilation. For location-less diagnostics about metadata types, re-anchor them at the consuming member (callerSymbol) or keep them at Location.None, depending on the human decision below.

findings.title: New tests skip generated-source checks and pin the silent-drop behaviour
findings.body: All three new tests set SkipGeneratedSourcesCheck and assert only that a resolver hint name exists and that no diagnostics appear. Nothing pins which formatters app generates for the referenced generic type, or that the output handles Item<int> correctly; the other tests in this file use Resources snapshots for that. The UnkeyedMember test asserts that an invalid referenced type yields zero diagnostics, so the dropped Error diagnostic becomes the expected behaviour. No new test exercises the F3.H2 change (it only runs in the analyzer when a Key value is null) or the `ContainsSyntaxTree` branch for a project reference.
findings.scenario: Reverting F3.H2 should leave all three new tests passing, because none of them reaches that line. Likewise, changing the generator to emit a resolver with no formatter for MyGenericStruct<int> would still satisfy `Assert.Contains(expectedResolverHintName, hintNames)` as long as the output compiles.
findings.suggestion: Add Resources snapshots, or at least assert that the generated resolver registers a formatter for the closed generic. Add a test using TestState.AdditionalProjects (project reference) for the ContainsSyntaxTree branch, and a metadata case that reaches the F3.H2 line. Add a test showing a same-project generic struct with an unkeyed member still reports MsgPack004 at its identifier.

findings.title: Docs promise the defining assembly reports the diagnostics, which the code cannot guarantee
findings.body: README and MsgPack004.md state that problems in a referenced-assembly type "are reported by the assembly that defines it". That holds only if the defining assembly was built with this analyzer enabled. The PR's own UnkeyedMember test compiles such a library with a bare CSharpCompilation and gets no diagnostic. The note is also placed only under MsgPack004, while the filter suppresses every analyzer ID TypeCollector reports, including MsgPack003 and the constructor diagnostics.
findings.scenario: A user consumes a NuGet package built without the analyzer (or with the diagnostic suppressed) that has an invalid generic [MessagePackObject] type. The docs say the defining project reports it, but no build reports anything.

refs.quote: Diagnostics about the members of such a type are reported by the assembly that defines it rather than by the consuming project, so any problem must be fixed there.
Members of a type defined in a referenced assembly are reported by the project that defines that type, so an unattributed public member of such a type must be fixed in its defining project.

findings.suggestion: Reword to say the consuming project does not report these, and that they appear only when the defining project runs the MessagePack analyzer. Put the note somewhere that covers all affected diagnostic IDs, not just MsgPack004.

discarded.title: MsgPack004 doc claims the analyzer never reports on referenced-assembly members
discarded.claimed: The new doc text says MsgPack004 only reports on members declared in the project being compiled. The inherited-member branch still reports BaseTypeContainsUnattributedPublicMembers, which uses the same MsgPack004 ID, at the base-type reference in the consuming project. That diagnostic is in source, so the new filter lets it through. The documented rule is therefore wrong for inherited members.
discarded.detail: Same defect as "Docs promise the defining assembly reports the diagnostics, which the code cannot guarantee" (raised by the surface lens); merged.

refusals.question: When an analyzer diagnostic applies to a type or member from a referenced assembly, should the consuming build drop it, report it at the consuming member, or report it without a location?
refusals.why: The requirement explicitly leaves this open. It decides whether a consumer sees anything when a referenced type is mis-attributed, which is a product and risk-appetite call. The reporter's core complaint was a silent failure.

options.label: Drop it silently
options.consequence: The consuming build is clean. Problems in referenced generic types (unkeyed members, no usable constructor, a missing [MessagePackObject] on a nested generic) surface only if the defining project runs the analyzer; otherwise they surface at runtime or as generated-code compile errors.

options.label: Report at the consuming member's location
options.consequence: The consumer sees an actionable diagnostic on its own member. It may be an error the consumer cannot fix without changing the referenced assembly, which can break builds that currently pass for generic classes.
options.implementedWhy: TypeCollector.cs:1077 and 1434 pass the metadata member's null location; callerSymbol is not used as a fallback.

refusals.context: The filter wraps every diagnostic the collector reports, not only the three former crash sites. The new test ClosedGenericStruct_FromMetadataReference_UnkeyedMember asserts zero diagnostics for a referenced struct with an unkeyed public property, which locks in the drop behaviour. README.md and MsgPack004.md now document it as intended. Error-severity analyzer diagnostics newly reported in consuming projects would be a visible compatibility change.

refs.quote: Diagnostics about the members of such a type are reported by the assembly that defines it rather than by the consuming project, so any problem must be fixed there.

refusals.question: Should the consuming assembly keep analysing closed generic types from referenced assemblies and generating formatters for their definitions, or treat them as handled by the defining assembly?
refusals.why: The requirement leaves this open. It changes which assembly owns the formatter for a referenced generic type and what the generated resolver contains. That is a design and compatibility decision.

options.label: Keep collecting and generating in the consumer
options.consequence: The consumer's resolver includes a formatter for the referenced generic definition, as it already does for generic classes. Generation is based on metadata only, so it may omit members or reference inaccessible ones with no diagnostic.
options.implementedWhy: TypeCollector.cs:651-654 still calls GetObjectInfo and CollectCore(type.OriginalDefinition) for closed generics.

options.label: Skip referenced-assembly generics in the consumer
options.consequence: No crash and no duplicate formatter. The consumer then relies on the defining assembly's resolver being registered at runtime, which changes behaviour for existing users of generic classes from referenced assemblies.
options.implementedWhy: TypeCollector.cs:361-365 sends generic types to CollectGeneric before the IsInMetadata early return at line 367.

refusals.context: Non-generic metadata types already return early at line 367 and are neither analysed nor generated. Generic ones take the CollectGeneric path first. The existing comment at line 653 says the definition is collected on purpose when it is defined outside the target project.

notChecked.why: Tests use a full implementation image. Reference assemblies strip private fields from classes but keep them for structs, so visible members differ and results may differ.

notChecked.why: No test covers them. Metadata-imported private struct fields might produce uncompilable generated code.
